In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a mathematical and numerical methodology for the analysis of the interaction of a laminar flame with the end walls of a combustion chamber.

the development and implementation of a numerical technique that can be applied to the solution of a wide variety of problems in the area of combustion, and the application of that technique to the study of flame-end-wall interaction.
the development of a mathematical model that can be used to predict the behavior of a planar flame in a channel bounded by a cold parallel wall, with emphasis on the effects of the flame on the wall.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the jump conditions for all the first derivatives of the dependent flame variables across the thin-flame zone are determined by the local flame structure, the flame thickness, and the flame speed.
the jump conditions across thin flame are not simply the same as those of an inviscid discontinuity.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the jump conditions for all the first derivatives of the dependent (state) variables across the thin reaction zone can be obtained from the solution of a single nonlinear ordinary differential equation.
the jump conditions for first (spatial)-order derivatives of the dependent flame variables are obtained in closed form.
the jump conditions for all the first derivatives are obtained, which are then used to derive the equations governing the flow in the unburnt and burnt gas.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the jump conditions across a thin flame are not simply the usual Rankine-Hugoniot relations for a discontinuous flame, as is commonly assumed, but are instead more complicated relations that involve the derivatives of the dependent state variables.
the jump conditions across a thin flame, when it is subjected to a planar end-wall interaction, are different from the jump conditions across an isolated flame.

the jump conditions for all the dependent variables across a thin flame are nonlinear functions of the local flame speed, and that they are not necessarily equal to the corresponding values for a stationary flame.
